'''''Leucospermum cordifolium''''' is an upright, [[evergreen]] shrub of up to 1½ m (5 ft) high from the [[Proteaceae]]. The flower heads are globe-shape with a flattened top, {{convert|10–12|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, and are carried individually or with two or three together mostly at a right angle to its branch. The [[perianth]] is 3–3½ cm long, yellow, orange or crimson in color. From each flower emerges a 4½–6 cm (1.8–2.4 in) long style sticking out horizontally but curving upwards near the obliquely, shell-shaped, thicker [[pollen presenter]]. This gives each head the appearance of a pincushion. Its common name is '''ornamental pincushion''' in English and '''{{Lang|af|bobbejaanklou}}''' in [[Afrikaans]]. It flowers between the middle of July and the end of November. It naturally occurs near the south coast of the [[Western Cape]] province of South Africa. Varieties and hybrids of this species are used as cut flower and garden plant.<ref name=Rourke /><ref name=IDENT>{{cite web|website= Protea Atlas Project|title= Identifying Pincushions|url= https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/pincushid.htm}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI|title= Leucospermum cordifolium|url= http://pza.sanbi.org/leucospermum-cordifolium}}</ref>

== Description ==
''L. cordifolium'' is a rounded and spreading shrub of up to 1½ m (5 ft) high and {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} in diameter that has a single trunk at its base from which branches spread horizontally and often bend towards the ground. The flowering stems may be more or less erect or spreading {{convert|5–8|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter initially covered in short, fine, cringy hairs, which may go lost with age. The hard, green leaves are set alternately along the branches, more or less directed upwards, oval or heart-shaped with an entire margin near the flowers and bluntly oblong and with up to six bony teeth at the tip lower down, {{convert|2–8|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and 2–4½ cm (0.8–1.8 in) wide, softly hairy at first, becoming hairless.<ref name=Rourke />

The flower heads are set on [[Peduncle (botany)|stalk]] of up to 1½ cm (0.6 in) long, have a flattened globe-shape of {{convert|10–12|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, and are carried individually or with two or three together mostly at a right angle to its branch. The [[Receptacle (botany)|common base]] is narrowly conical in shape with a pointy tip 3–3½ cm (1.2–1.4 in) long and ¾ cm (0.3 in) wide. The bracts that subtend the flower head consists of oval [[bract]]s with a pointy tip of {{convert|4–5|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide and about {{convert|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, overlapping and pressed against the common base, rubbery and with some short and soft hair. The bracts at the foot of each individual flower are concave, embrace the [[perianth]] at its base, have a pointy, incurved tip {{convert|8–10|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and about {{convert|7|mm|abbr=on}} wide, with a rubbery consistency and thickly woolly at its base.<ref name=Rourke />

The perianth is 3–3½ cm long, yellow, orange or crimson in color. The cylindric perianth tube is hairless and {{convert|8–10|mm|in|abbr=on}}. The three periant lobes at the side of the centre of the flowerhead remain united and form a hairless, rolled sheath, except for some rigid hairs on the margins. The lobe facing towards the rim of the flowerhead is free. The [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] are ovate and sit atop a {{convert|1|mm|in|abbr=on}} long filament. The [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] is 4½–6 cm (1.8–2.4 in) long, sticking out horizontally but curving upwards near the obliquely shell-shaped [[pollen presenter]], with a flattened tip that also contains an oblique groove that functions as the [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]]. Subtending the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] are four awl-shaped scales of about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Rourke />

The subtribe Proteinae, to which the genus ''Leucospermum'' has been assigned, consistently has a basic chromosome number of twelve ([[Diploid|2n]]=24).<ref>{{cite journal|first1= L.A.S.|last1= Johnson|first2= Barbara G.|last2= Briggs|year= 1975|title= On the Proteaceae—the evolution and classification of a southern family|journal= Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume= 70|issue= 2|page= 106|doi= 10.1111/j.1095-8339.1975.tb01644.x}}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

=== Differences with related species ===
The ornamental pincushion can be distinguished by its spreading habit, with horizontal branches, leaf-shapes that range from oblong with teeth in the earliest growth of the season to entire and oval closer to the flower heads. The flower heads are generally at a right angle to the branch it grows from, on the perianth lobes are only some soft hairs and the pollen presenter has a skewed shell shape. The closely related ''[[Leucospermum patersonii|L. patersonii]]'' is more tree-like, with larger, less variable, broadly oblong leaves that consistently have three to eight teeth near the tip, woolly perianth lobes and upright flower heads.<ref name=Rourke />

== Taxonomy ==
In 1809, [[Joseph Knight (horticulturist)|Joseph Knight]] published a book titled ''[[On the cultivation of the plants belonging to the natural order of Proteeae]]'', that contained an extensive revision of the [[Proteaceae]] attributed to [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]]. Salisbury was the first to describe the ornamental pincushion and named it ''Leucadendrum cordifolium''. In 1900 however, his generic names were [[Conserved name|suppressed]] in favour of those proposed by [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]]. Robert Brown called the species ''Leucospermum nutans'' in 1810. In 1841, the French botanist [[Jean Louis Marie Poiret|Jean Poiret]] moved the species and made the combination ''Protea nutans''. [[Otto Kuntze]] moved the species again, now to his genus ''Leucadendron'', making the combination ''Leucadendron nutans'' in 1891. Kuntze's genus however is a later synonym of ''Leucospermum'' by Brown, and a later [[Homonym (biology)|homonym]] of ''Leucadendron'' as proposed by Linnaeus. The species name proposed by Salisbury is the earliest and was not suppressed unlike his genus name. [[Edwin Percy Phillips]] described a slightly different form in 1910 and called it ''Leucospermum mixtum'', while a third form was named ''Leucospermum bolusii'', a later homonym of the name proposed by Michel Gandoger in 1901 for [[Leucospermum bolusii|another species]]. ''Leucospermum integrifolium'' was described by Gandoger and [[Hans Schinz]] in 1913, and ''Leucospermum meisneri'' by Gandoger that same year. In 1932, [[Henry Georges Fourcade]] realised the [[new combination]] ''Leucospermum cordifolium'' needed to be made. [[John Patrick Rourke]] in 1970 considered all of these names [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] of ''Leucospermum cordifolium''.<ref name=Rourke />

''L. cordifolium'' has been assigned to the showy pincushions, section ''[[Leucospermum#Brevifilamentum|Brevifilamentum]]''.<ref name=PAP>{{cite web|website= Protea Atlas Project|title= Showy pincushions|url= https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/pincush3.htm}}</ref>

The species name ''cordifolium'' is compounded from the [[Latin]] words ''cordis'' meaning "heart" and ''folium'' meaning "leaf", so heart-shaped leaf.<ref name=Criley>{{cite book|first= Richard A.|last= Criley|year= 2010|chapter= 2|title= Leucospermum: Botany and Horticulture|series= Horticultural Reviews|volume= 61|editor= Jules Janick|publisher= John Wiley & Sons|isbn= 978-0-470-65072-1|chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=lVlilno_NacC&pg=PA34}}</ref>

== Distribution, habitat and ecology ==
''Leucospermum cordifolium'' can be found in a strip between Soetanysberg, [[Bredasdorp]], [[Elim, Western Cape|Elim]] and [[Napier, Western Cape]] in the southeast, through [[Stanford, Western Cape|Stanford]], [[Caledon, Western Cape|Caledon]], [[Onrusrivier]] and [[Botrivier]], to Aries Kraal in the northwest, in the foothills of the [[Kogelberg]]. Unlike close relative ''[[Leucospermum patersonii|L. patersonii]]'' that is confined to limestone ridges, ''L. cordifolium'' can only be found on acid soils that derived from [[Table Mountain Sandstone]]. Groups or individuals
grow in open, hilly terrain at 30–450 m (100–1500 ft) in a [[fynbos]] vegetation that mostly consist of other [[Proteaceae]], several [[Erica (plant)|Erica]] species and [[Restionaceae]]. Along its distribution area, the average annual precipitation is 625–1025 mm (15–40 in), which predominantly falls during the winter half year.<ref name=Rourke />

The ornamental pincushion is pollinated by birds. The ripe fruits fall to the ground about two months after flowering. Here these are collected by native ants that carry them to their underground nests. Here the seeds remain protected against fire, seed-eating rodents and birds. After a fire has cleared the vegetation cover, increased daily temperature fluctuations and chemicals from charred wood seeping to the seeds with the rain, promote germination and so revives the pincushion at these locations.<ref name=PAP /><ref>{{cite web|website= Gondwana Game Reserve|title= Leucospermum cordifolium, the ants and the fire|url= http://www.gondwanagr.co.za/leucospermum-cordifolium-ants-fire/}}</ref> Tests showed that germination is best with the temperature fluctuating daily between {{Convert|9 and 24|C}}, which corresponds to the micro climate during winter in its home range after the vegetation has been cleared.<ref>{{cite journal|first= G.J.|last= Brits|year= 1986|title= Influence of fluctuating temperatures and H2O2 treatment on germination of Leucospermum cordifolium and Serruina florida (Proteaceae) seeds|journal= [[South African Journal of Botany]]|volume= 52|issue= 4|pages= 286–290|doi= 10.1016/S0254-6299(16)31522-8|doi-access= free}}</ref>
